title: Paying attention
subtitle: Selecting a little, discarding a lot
question: What happens when you concentrate on one thing?
teaser: Count the blue ones. Then find out what you missed while counting.
intro: Attention usually gets described as a spotlight. It is closer to a competition. Lots of things are being processed at once, and attention is what tips the contest toward whatever matters right now. The price of winning that contest is everything else.

events.title: A goal is held
events.explanation: 'Count the blue ones' has to be actively held in mind for the whole task. Nothing stores it for you.
events.science: Goal maintenance is effortful and decays. This is why instructions are lost when a task runs long or when something interrupts.

events.title: The goal becomes a spatial priority
events.explanation: The front of your brain turns that goal into a bias — toward certain places, and toward the colour blue.

events.title: A priority map forms
events.explanation: A running ranking forms of what matters where. Not what is brightest; what is relevant.
events.science: 'Priority map' is a computational description. It is supported by the way parietal activity tracks behavioural relevance rather than raw stimulus intensity.

events.title: Early vision is retuned
events.explanation: Your visual system is retuned before anything appears. Blue things, wherever they are, will now get a head start.
events.science: Attentional modulation of early visual cortex is measurable in the absence of any stimulus change. Attention changes the receiver, not just the selection.

events.title: Feature bias
events.explanation: The bias is for the colour itself, across the whole display — not just one spot.

events.title: The scene arrives
events.explanation: Everything on screen gets processed. Attention does not stop things entering. It decides which ones win.

events.title: Competition
events.explanation: Targets and distractors compete. The ones you biased get an advantage and push the others down.
events.science: Biased-competition accounts explain why two objects in the same receptive field interfere with each other, and why attending to one largely removes the interference.

events.title: Tracking and counting
events.explanation: Keeping a running count means holding a number and updating it while everything keeps moving. That is real work.

events.title: Global gain
events.explanation: How alert you are changes how strongly the whole brain responds. A setting, not a message.

events.title: What was suppressed
events.explanation: The things that lost were still built. They just never got strong enough for you to be able to report them.
events.science: This is the standard account of inattentional blindness: the unattended event was processed to some depth, but never won access to the systems that would let you report it.

events.title: An interruption
events.explanation: Something unexpected and attention-grabbing appears. A more automatic system reacts and signals that your goal might be wrong.

events.title: Reorienting
events.explanation: Priority shifts. The count you were holding becomes the first thing likely to get dropped.

events.title: Back to the task
events.explanation: The goal gets put back. Putting it back is not free — that is where the cost of being interrupted comes from.

causalChain.label: A goal is held
causalChain.detail: The instruction has to be actively held. It fades if nothing holds it.

causalChain.label: The goal becomes a bias
causalChain.detail: That goal gets turned into a bias toward certain places and features.

causalChain.label: Sensory cortex is retuned
causalChain.detail: Your visual system is retuned before the display even appears.

causalChain.label: Everything is processed
causalChain.detail: Everything gets processed. Attention does not block things at the door.

causalChain.label: Biased competition resolves
causalChain.detail: The biased things win the competition and reach the point where you can report them.

causalChain.label: The losers stay invisible
causalChain.detail: The losers were built and thrown away. You cannot report something that never won.

causalChain.label: Interruption overrides the goal
causalChain.detail: A surprising event can force the whole thing to be reallocated, whatever you intended.

science.text: Attending to a location or feature increases responses in visual cortex to stimuli matching that location or feature.
People routinely fail to report salient, unexpected events while performing an attentionally demanding task — a robust and widely replicated finding.
Frontal and parietal regions are reliably engaged during goal-directed attention tasks, and a more ventral, right-lateralised network responds to unexpected relevant events.
We separate 'goal-directed' and 'stimulus-driven' attention into two clean systems. The two interact continuously and share nodes.
The spotlight metaphor is used in the interface because it is intuitive. Biased competition is the better description, and is what the simulation actually illustrates.
Attention is not a substance you have a limited amount of. Describing it as a resource is a useful shorthand for a competitive process, not a claim about brain fuel.
The levels shown are generated by this scenario file. Nothing here measures your attention.

references.label: Biased competition
references.note: An account in which attention resolves competition between simultaneously active representations rather than filtering input.

references.label: Inattentional blindness
references.note: Classic demonstrations that observers engaged in a counting task fail to notice conspicuous unexpected events.

references.label: Dorsal and ventral attention networks
references.note: A framework distinguishing goal-directed orienting from stimulus-driven reorienting.

readouts.label: Target selectivity
readouts.note: How strongly the things you are looking for beat the things you are not.

readouts.label: Chance of missing the unexpected
readouts.note: How likely you are to miss something unexpected. Concentrating harder makes this worse, not better.

readouts.label: Recovery after interruption
readouts.note: How easily you get back on task after something pulls you away.

outcome.headline: Attending
outcome.body: Holding a goal changed how your eyes and brain responded before anything appeared. The things you did not count were not blocked at the door — they were built, they lost, and they were thrown away.
outcome.insight: The sharper your focus, the more you miss. That is not a fault in the system. That is what choosing means.
